content.comment_body: I've been working on a program for a [product_name] PLC with [article_no] for weeks. A decision was made to switch to [article_no], so I changed the hardware type in [product_name] to the new [article_no]. I'm using [version_no] of [product_name]. I want to run the program on either model, but when I try switching back, I get a message: "ck name exceeds 8 characters, unable to change to lower hardware versions." I assume 'ck' stands for 'check'? None of my block names are over 8 characters, so I'm unsure what else it could reference. Also, does a counter with no reset retain its value indefinitely, or only until the PLC memory expires (after several days without power)?
This refers to the length of the block name. Please check the video attached.
If the counter is set as retentive, the value remains until you either reset the counter or upload a new program. With retentivity enabled, the count is stored in flash memory.
None of my block names exceed 8 characters. Some of my "M" flags do, but the program has worked on the previous [product_name] PLC for weeks.
How long does the flash memory retain data after power is lost?
Please upload your program. Without seeing it, it's difficult to diagnose.
It lasts longer than a human lifetime.
I've sent the program to you via email.
You're misleading me. There's a block with a name longer than 8 characters. Block T033 'INDARMFLSH' is 10 characters, 2 more than allowed.
I can't believe I missed that! Thanks!

analysis.insight_summary: Users are confused and frustrated when switching projects between hardware versions in [product_name] software, mainly due to unclear error messages. The restriction on block name length for certain hardware models is insufficiently explained and ambiguously enforced in the software. This results in users struggling to pinpoint compatibility issues and requirements.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect to transition programs easily between hardware types and want straightforward, actionable error messages about compatibility. They also expect details about data retention features (such as counters) within the PLC to be clearly documented, regardless of the hardware version.
